Welcome to the data center infrastructure
that keeps the digital world

running. In this lesson, we'll explore the
key physical

components at a high level that make a
data center function: power,

cooling, and layout. Let's imagine a data
center building

and dissect the key components from the
outside in. The first

layers include power and cooling
facilities. We'll start with power.

Data centers have powerful energy systems
designed to keep operations running
24/7, 365 days a year. From

generators and UPSes, batteries, to
distribution switchgear,

the power infrastructure is a critical
system that supplies energy to all the

equipment in the data center. Now on to
the cooling infrastructure.

Chillers, condensers, and air handling
units that help manage temperature

and humidity on the data center floor so
that the systems don't

overheat or shut down. These systems don't
work in

isolation. Every part of the data center
is connected through cables,

power rails, busways, and energy
management systems. They

ensure that power is delivered efficiently
to the rack. Then

comes rack level distribution. This is
where the

actual compute happens, and a lot of the
energy is consumed and heat is

generated. Servers are arranged in
enclosures where hot and cold

air is separated. Cooling via localized
air or liquid

is constantly monitored with smart sensors
and software. All

of this is maintained and monitored by
systems that

control real-time adjustments, alarm, and
automation.

Think of it as the nervous center of the
data center. In the

next lesson, we'll go deeper into specific
subsystems like power and

cooling, but now you should have a
bird's-eye view of how all

the parts come together to create an
always-on environment.

cues.text:
So, now that you understand how data
drives the digital world,

let's answer the big question. What
exactly is a data

center? In simple terms, a data center is
a specialized

facility that houses computing systems,
servers, storage,

and networking hardware. These systems
support everything

from websites and cloud services to
enterprise apps, financial

transactions, and even the AI models we
work with.

You can think of it like this. When you
stream a movie, check your bank

account, join a video call, you're
reaching out to computers

located somewhere in the world inside a
data center.

But a data center is much more than just a
room full of computers.

It's a tightly controlled environment
designed to maximize uptime,

performance, security, all the time being
as

efficient as possible. First, there's
power.

Servers don't just plug into the wall.
Data centers use

redundant power systems. They use backup
generators and

battery arrays to keep everything running
even during outages.

Then there's cooling. Servers compute a
lot of information,
and that generates heat, a lot of it.

So data centers use air and even liquid
cooling systems

to cool server components and maintain
ideal operating

temperatures for these servers to run
reliably and at full speed.

Connectivity is another key layer. Data
centers act as digital

hubs connected to the Internet via high-
speed fiber optic cables.

Many of these are also carrier neutral,
meaning they connect to multiple

providers offering maximum connectivity
options.

Security is baked into every level,
physical and digital. Think of

biometric access, surveillance, and fire
suppression physically.

Firewall segmentation and threat detection
are done digitally

and physically. All together, these
systems

create an environment where critical data
and applications can live safely,
operate continuously, and scale as needed.

But not all data centers are the same.
They vary in size,

purpose, and location. In fact, you can
think of data
centers as existing on a spectrum. Smaller

ones typically serve individual businesses
and enterprises,

while larger ones, hyperscale facilities,
support
vast global cloud platforms. Some
serve small regional businesses. Others,

and they are called hyperscale data
centers, are run by tech giants like

Amazon, Google, or Microsoft, and they
support global
cloud services. Then there are also

edge data centers. They're smaller,
modular units

placed closer to where the data is
generated. These are vital for real-time
services like IoT, 5G, and AI.

Regardless of size, all data centers share
the same goal,

to efficiently process, store, and move
massive
volumes of data reliably, fast, and
securely. So why does this matter? Well,

while we may not see them, data centers
are essential to the

smooth operation of our daily digital
world.

Data centers are the invisible backbone of
everything we do online.

They allow companies to scale, innovate,
and operate globally.

Without data centers, the digital world
simply wouldn't

function. In the next chapter, we'll take
a closer look

inside a data center to explore the key
elements in the physical
infrastructure that powers it all.

When you picture a data center, what comes
to mind? Maybe a secure

building with rows of servers glowing in
green light. That's not wrong,

but it's only the surface. Data centers
are engineered

ecosystems optimized for nonstop digital
operations.

In this video, we'll take a look at how
they're physically structured from

the ground up. The first thing to
understand is that

everything in a data center is built for
maximum uptime. Whether you're

streaming a video, sending an email, or
just using cloud

applications somewhere, a data center is
powering that

experience. To stay online twenty-four
seven,

a data center needs three core systems,
and they all work together.
They're power, cooling, and IT equipment.

Let's start with cooling because heat is
one of the biggest

enemies of performance. Data centers
generate a lot

of heat. On the outside, you'll see
industrial-grade chillers,

condensers, and cooling towers. These
systems work

to remove heat from the building through a
mix of air and liquid cold

methods. Inside, air handling units, also
known as CRACs,

Computer Room Air Conditioners, keep
temperatures in check by distributing

cold air across the data hall. For liquid-
cooled servers,

cooling distribution units, or CDUs,
ensure cold

liquid keeps the servers cool. These
systems

often operate in tandem with raised floors
and cold aisle

containments. They also include smart
sensors. Now let's talk

about power. At the heart of any data
center is an incredibly robust

energy system. Power typically enters from
utility

lines from the grid or renewable sources
and runs through medium and low

voltage switchgear. From here, it's fed
via backup
systems, diesel generators, and UPSs, or

uninterruptible power supplies for short.
These are banks of

batteries and help keep the data center
running during

outages or grid instability. Once
stabilized,

power is distributed through PDUs, or
power distribution

units, and sometimes even intelligent
busbars that reduce
complexity in cable routing. All of this

ensures that each server receives
consistent, safe

electricity. The layout of a data center
also

plays a major role. Most are designed with
hot and cold aisle containments

to keep airflow controlled and cooling
efficient. Sensors track

temperature, humidity, and power usage in
real time.

Centralized control systems allow
technicians to automate responses and

optimize system performance remotely.
Increasingly, data

centers are becoming more sustainable.
Some include microgrids,

solar panels, or fuel cell systems to
reduce reliance on

public utilities and carbon output. Rack-
level equipment

has also evolved. Racks are designed not
only for high-density

performance but also for efficient
airflow, liquid cooling,

cable management, and environmental
sensing.

All these systems, cooling, power, and
monitoring, are

coordinated to keep the data center
reliable and secure.

Downtime isn't an option when you're
supporting financial markets, hospitals,

or global communication platforms. So to
summarize,

data centers are more than just rows of
servers.

They are intricately designed
infrastructures combining engineering,
IT, and environmental controls. Each

component, chillers, batteries, busbars,
and racks, has a

role in keeping your digital world up and
running. In the

next lesson, we'll zoom in on how data
centers handle power

distribution and why energy systems are
one of the most
critical components in digital operations.

cues.text:
Imagine a hundred megawatt data center.
Just to turn on the

lights, run servers, and maintain a stable
environment requires

a massive and uninterrupted supply of
electricity.

In this video, we'll explore how power
flows into a data center

and what keeps it running even when the
grid goes down.

Power begins at the utility level.
Electricity is generated,

transmitted through the grid, and routed
to a substation. From

there, voltage is stepped down and
delivered to the data

center through dedicated high-capacity
lines. Once it

reaches the facility, the first stop is
the input switchgear.

This equipment acts as a control hub,
distributing power to

critical systems and protecting them from
faults. Power

then flows into uninterruptible power
supplies or UPS
units. These systems maintain power during
brief outages or surges. If the grid cuts
out, UPS batteries provide power

instantaneously and offer a buffer of
power to keep systems

online just long enough for generators to
activate.

Next are the backup generators. They often
run on diesel or HVO.

HVO is a more sustainable fuel than
diesel, and it's short for

hydrotreated vegetable oil. Now, these
generators are

on continuously. They're always on
standby, and they

automatically supply full operational
power within seconds

of an outage. Many data centers also use
redundant

generator systems for added resilience.
Once

stabilized, power moves through redundant
feeds across the data centers

to the PDUs, the power distribution units.
These act like circuit

breaker panels for the data center. They
allocate electricity to the various

systems in the IT rack, servers, storage
units,

or networking switchgear. PDUs ensure that
every

device down to the server level receives
consistent power.

They also allow for monitoring and real-
time adjustments.

Power density has become a major topic. A
few years ago,

the average rack might draw four or five
kilowatts

of power. Today, it's common to see
fifteen, thirty,

or even a hundred kilowatts of power usage
per rack. For the near

future, some projections go as far as four
hundred kilowatts or even

one megawatt. Now, these power densities
are mostly driven by

the adoption of high-performance workloads
such as AI.

In daily operations, this entire
architecture runs in

harmony, but when something fails, it's
the coordination

between management tools, UPS systems,
switchgear, and

backup generators that prevents downtime.
Power in a
data center is not just about electricity.

It's about providing that power
continuously. It's about

providing redundancy and proactive
management.

Every second of uptime is critical,
whether it's

for financial markets, healthcare,
government, or your
cloud applications.

cues.text:
In every data center, cooling is just as
critical as power.

Servers and networking equipment generate
heat continuously,

and if that heat isn't removed, equipment
performance can suffer

or, worse, fail completely. That's why
modern data centers

are engineered with robust cooling
systems. These systems work to

extract and dissipate heat efficiently,
maintaining the

optimal operating temperature and ensuring
reliable uptime.

So how do these systems work? First, let's
take a look at the heat

cycle. Heat is produced inside the servers
and

transferred via the air through components
like fans or heat exchangers.

The goal is to move the heat out of the
data center as efficient as

possible. One of the most common systems
is air

cooling. This uses fans or computer room
air

conditioning units, CRACs, to circulate
air across hot

equipment. The warm air is then moved away
and cooled,

either through chilled water systems or
refrigerants. Another

approach is liquid cooling, which has
become more popular

with the increase in high-performance
computing. These

systems use coolants, typically dielectric
or

water-like fluids, to absorb heat directly
from the hardware.

In liquid cooling systems, cold liquid
flows close to the

processor and other components. They
absorb the heat

and transport it away to be cooled again,
often using

external heat exchangers or chillers. Data
centers

may also use evaporative cooling, also
known as

adiabatic cooling as well. This method
cools air by

allowing water to evaporate into it. It's
energy

efficient and particularly useful in
regions with dry climates.

Another emerging cooling technology with
liquid

cooling is immersion cooling. This is
where servers are

fully submerged in a non-conductive
liquid. This

liquid fully absorbs the heat directly
from the hardware, offering

high efficient thermal transfers.
Immersion cooling

reduces the need for mechanical fans. It
cuts energy use and is

ideal for high-density computing, such as
AI
workloads. Now, let's consider where

this cooling is happening. Cooling can be
implemented at

different levels: component level, rack
level, room level, and

building level. Each level adds a layer of
redundancy

and control. At the room level, hot and
cold

aisles are often used. This technique
arranges servers in a way that

hot air is exhausted into one aisle while
cold

air is directly into another, avoiding
mixing the

two. From a systems view, heat is
collected and

transported and rejected outside the data
center building

using chillers, condensers, and cooling
towers.

Now, let's consider a power outage. During
such

events, cooling systems, like IT systems,
must remain

operational. That's why they're often
connected to backup

power sources like UPS systems or diesel
generators to

ensure continuity. Without adequate
cooling,

even for a short time, equipment can reach
critical temperatures

quickly. This could lead to thermal
throttling or sudden
shutdowns, risking data loss or, worse,

hardware damage. In today's high-density
environments, cooling is

about performance, efficiency, and
reliability.

Engineers must balance cooling capacity
with energy use

to optimize both operational cost and
environmental

impact. One emerging strategy for
improving data center

efficiency is to increase the thermal set
point, the temperature at

which cooling systems begin operation.
According to

ASHRAE guidelines, modern equipment can
safely operate at higher

inlet temperatures, often up to twenty-
seven degrees

or eighty degrees Fahrenheit. By designing
around these higher

temperatures or set points, data centers
can reduce

reliance on mechanical cooling. They can
lower energy uses

and lower their environmental impact. As
data

centers grow and computing needs
intensifies, smarter

and more sustainable cooling approaches
like liquid cooling,

evaporative methods, and higher set points
will become essential.

They not only protect the equipment, but
also help organizations meet energy
efficiency and climate goals.

3.5 inches tall, while 2-socket means it
can hold two
CPUs or processors. These processors work

together to handle high-performance tasks.

a power supply unit, hard drives or SSDs,

It performs the calculations and
instructions that drive applications.

It's paired with a heat sink and fans to
manage the heat it generates.

Memory, or RAM, stores active data so the
CPU

can quickly access it. Servers also
include

PCIe expansion slots, which connect to the

bus. It's a high-speed pathway that allows

for artificial intelligence processing,

or high-performance sto- storage

components dramatically increase a

performance in specialized workloads.

need fast, reliable storage. Hard drives
and

solid-state drives, or SSDs, are used

high-transaction environments. Traditional
spindle hard

drives offer more capacity for a lower
price but have lower performance

and require more power. And because they
have mechanical parts,

they are more likely to fail faster than

supply is a critical component. It

to ensure reliability. Cooling is another

part of the IT infrastructure. Air flows

aisle, typically through perforated tiles

ensures components stay within optimal

Beyond servers, data centers rely on other

Networking equipment like routers and

Storage appliances manage vast amounts of
data,
structured and unstructured. Increasingly,

AI servers are also being developed. These
are

high-powered machines equipped with
specialized GPUs to handle workloads like

machine learning and advanced analytics.
They typically require

higher power and cooling capacity. All of
these

systems must be highly connected and
redundant.

Redundant power feeds, network paths, and
component backups ensure

continuous uptime in servers. These
redundant

architectures and connectivity are what

It's roughly 3.5 inches tall, while 2-socket means it can hold two CPUs or processors. These processors work together to handle high-performance tasks. Inside the server, we'll find several key components: the CPU, the heat sink, memory modules, PCIe cards for expansion, a power supply unit, hard drives or SSDs, and multiple cooling fans. These components all work together to process, store, and transmit data across the network. The CPU, or processor, is the brain of the server. It performs the calculations and instructions that drive applications. It's paired with a heat sink and fans to manage the heat it generates. Memory, or RAM, stores active data so the CPU can quickly access it. Servers also include PCIe expansion slots, which connect to the PCIe bus. It's a high-speed pathway that allows the server to add extra capabilities. This might include GPUs for artificial intelligence processing, network interface cards, or high-performance sto- storage controllers. These components dramatically increase a server's flexibility and performance in specialized workloads. Servers also need fast, reliable storage. Hard drives and solid-state drives, or SSDs, are used depending on the performance needs. SSDs offer faster access times and better durability, making them ideal for high-transaction environments. Traditional spindle hard drives offer more capacity for a lower price but have lower performance and require more power.
